Olga de Amaral: Olga de Amaral was born as Olga Ceballos Velez in Bogotá, Cundinamarca, Colombia to parents from the Antioquia region of Colombia.
Olga de Amaral: She was raised in a traditional religious family with 5 sisters and 2 brothers.
Olga de Amaral: She grew up in a traditional neighbourhood in Bogotá in a warm, safe family atmosphere, maintaining a special relationship with her loving and caring mother.
Olga de Amaral: Upon graduating from high school, in the years 1951-52 she got a degree in Architectural Design at the Colegio Mayor de Cundinamarca in Bogotá.
Olga de Amaral: After graduation, the future textile artist worked for a year as a director of the Architectural Drawing Faculty at the same school.
Olga de Amaral: In 1954, de Amaral went to the United States to study English in New York at the Columbia University.
Olga de Amaral: She then moved and studied fiber art at the Cranbrook Academy of Art in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, USA (1954–55).

Olga de Amaral: The artist cherishes that period of her education and considers it crucial for her later artistic development: "In Cranbrook, the textile workshop had eight looms placed against the windows: one of them, in the corner, would be my home for a year.
Olga de Amaral: There, I lived my most intimate moments of solitude; there was born my certainty about color; its strength; I felt as if I loved color as though it were something tangible.
Olga de Amaral: I also learned to speak in color.
Olga de Amaral: I remember with nostalgia that experience in which souls touched hands".
Olga de Amaral: At Cranbrook de Amaral met Jim Amaral and they became close friends.
Olga de Amaral: In 1955, after a year in Cranbrook, she returned to Colombia and started to make decorative textiles on commission for her architect friends.
Olga de Amaral: Meanwhile, Jim Amaral was in the U.S. Navy, on a base in the Philippines.
Olga de Amaral: In 1956, Jim visited Colombia to see Olga, initially for a few weeks.
Olga de Amaral: Shortly after, Jim Amaral and Olga Ceballos Velez married and settled in Bogotá.
Olga de Amaral: They started a family (children Diego and Andrea) and a workshop of handwoven textiles.
Olga de Amaral: During that period, Jack Lenor Larsen visited Colombia and the Amaral's workshop.
Olga de Amaral: He expressed interest in Olga's tapestries.
Olga de Amaral: Their professional and artistic relationship became crucial in projection of her work internationally in the world of contemporary tapestry.
Olga de Amaral: In 1965 de Amaral founded and taught at the Textile Department at the Universidad de los Andes (University of the Andes) in Bogotá.
Olga de Amaral: In 1966-1967 the Amaral family lived in New York.
Olga de Amaral: There Olga de Amaral met Eileen Vanderbilt from the World Crafts Council and became its representative for Colombia.

Olga de Amaral: With Jack Lenor Larsen's collaboration, Olga de Amaral displayed her tapestries in New York (solo exhibition in Jack Lenor Larsen’s New York showroom in 1967), taught at Penland School of Crafts in North Carolina and in Haystack Mountain School of Crafts in Maine.
Olga de Amaral: After returning to Colombia, the Amarals travelled to Popayán and Tierradentro region with its must-see San Agustín.
Olga de Amaral: Later Olga visited Peru as the WCC representative.
Olga de Amaral: On a rapid visit to Ireland to participate in a WCC conference, Olga met Lucie Rie, a British ceramist who inspired her to incorporate gold into the tapestries.
Olga de Amaral: At the beginning of the seventies, the Amarals moved to Barcelona and then to Paris.
Olga de Amaral: They visited Greece, Italy, Holland, Belgium, Switzerland, Sweden, and England.
Olga de Amaral: They made contacts with the centres of European art.
Olga de Amaral: They lived for a time in Europe, then returned to Bogotá, visited different areas of Colombia, and then went back to France, amid exhibits, work, and new friendships.
Olga de Amaral: Another important journey for the artist was her travel to Japan.
Olga de Amaral: Nowadays Olga de Amaral lives and works in Bogotá, Colombia.

Henry C. Groseclose: Henry C. Groseclose was born on May 17, 1892.
Henry C. Groseclose: He lived in Ceres, Virginia for most of his life.
Henry C. Groseclose: Mr. Groseclose completed his junior college degree from Washington and Lee University in 1917.
Henry C. Groseclose: In his later years, he also received his bachelor’s degree, as well as his master’s degree, in agricultural education from Virginia Tech.

Henry C. Groseclose: While Mr. Groseclose was an agriculture teacher at the Virginia Polytechnic Institute, he, along with three other agriculture teachers, Walter Newman, Edmund Magill and Harry Sanders, decided to establish a club for the farm boys in the school.
Henry C. Groseclose: The organization was fired up in 1925.
Henry C. Groseclose: Groseclose named the organization the Future Farmers of Virginia, or FFV for short.
Henry C. Groseclose: The original meaning for the abbreviation FFV stood for the First Families of Virginia.
Henry C. Groseclose: The “first families” referred to the families of both George Washington and Thomas Jefferson.

Henry C. Groseclose: Referring to Washington and Jefferson, Groseclose once stated that, “The Future Farmers of America should follow the example of these great sons of early Virginia by using scientific knowledge, intelligence, and enthusiasm to the end that agriculture may again be known as the profession of the real aristocrat.”
Henry C. Groseclose: Groseclose wrote the by-laws, as well as the constitution that the FFV would be based on.
Henry C. Groseclose: In 1926, he also wrote, and brought into play, the formal ceremony that would take place as an organizational pattern to structure each meeting.
Henry C. Groseclose: Two years later, in 1928, the FFV became a nationwide organization.
Henry C. Groseclose: This developed the organization that is known today as the Future Farmers of America, or The National FFA Organization, or just FFA for short.
Henry C. Groseclose: The by-laws drawn up by Henry Groseclose became the foundation of the newly national organization.
Henry C. Groseclose: Also, the formal ceremony that Groseclose developed was taken on by the FFA as a national ritual that is still used today.

Henry C. Groseclose: Groseclose was a seventh degree Grange member, and he was also involved with the Masons, so it was no surprise when he developed levels of memberships for the FFV, which transferred through to the FFA, that were similar to the three leveled membership structure that the Masons uses.
Henry C. Groseclose: These three levels included the Greenhand, the Virginia Farmer and the Virginia Planter.

Henry C. Groseclose: While the official emblem of the National FFA Organization was being drawn, Groseclose’s original emblem, which he hand drew himself, was highly considered and ended up playing a part in the emblem that is still the emblem of the National FFA Organization today.

Henry C. Groseclose: The part of the emblem that was from Mr. Groseclose’s original drawing included a background setting of a half plowed wheat field with an owl perched upon a spade of wheat in front of the field.
Henry C. Groseclose: Henry Groseclose served as the Executive Secretary of the National FFA Organization for two years between 1928 and 1930.

Henry C. Groseclose: During his office of Executive Secretary, he announced at the national convention of 1930 that he had written, and would be releasing, an official FFA manual, which outlined the organization, procedures and structures of the National FFA Organization.
Henry C. Groseclose: Mr. Groseclose also served as the Treasurer of the National FFA Organization for 11 years, between 1930 and 1941.

Henry C. Groseclose: In September 1925, Henry Groseclose set his expectations for the members of the FFV, and the purpose of the establishment of the Future Farmers of Virginia was by saying, "In my opinion the farm boys of Virginia who are enrolled in vocational agriculture are equal to any other group of boys in the state.
Henry C. Groseclose: But somehow the boys themselves seem to have a feeling of inferiority.
Henry C. Groseclose: Especially is this true when the farm boy goes to the city and has to compete with his city cousin.
Henry C. Groseclose: This condition should not exist.
Henry C. Groseclose: I believe that a strong organization of our boys in agriculture would help them to overcome this handicap.
Henry C. Groseclose: Let's form an organization that will give them a greater opportunity for self-expression and for the development of leadership.
Henry C. Groseclose: In this way they will develop confidence in their own ability and pride in the fact that they are farm boys."

Dirt track racing began in the United States before World War I and became widespread during the 1920s and 1930s.
Two different types of race cars dominated—open wheel racers in the Northeast and West and stock cars in the South.

While open wheel race cars are purpose-built racing vehicles, stock cars (also known as fendered cars) can be either purpose-built race cars or street vehicles that have been modified to varying degrees.

GS Consolat: Groupe sportif Consolat (sometimes referred to as Marseille Consolat) is a French amateur football club founded in 1964 and based in the Bouches-du-Rhone department of Marseille.
GS Consolat: The club is named after Consolat, a neighborhood located in La Calade, in the 15th arrondissement, north of Marseille.
GS Consolat: Founded in 1964 by the residents of Consolat, the club has been run by current club president Jean-Luc Mingallon since 1983.
GS Consolat: Mingallon pushed the team to success which has led to their promotion from the Division d’Honneur in 1999.
GS Consolat: In 2006, the club reached the national amateur level of football with its promotion to CFA2.
GS Consolat: This promotion sparked new derbies with the reserve team of Olympique de Marseille and US Endoume.
GS Consolat: The desire to become “the second club of Marseille” was one step closer with the promotion to the CFA in 2011.
GS Consolat: Consolat won the CFA title in 2014, earning promotion to the Championnat National, the third tier of French football.
GS Consolat: They nearly were promoted to Ligue 2 during the 2015-2016 season, falling short only by a single point behind Amiens SC.
GS Consolat: They again missed out on possible promotion in the following season, finishing behind division rivals Paris FC due only to goal differential.
